content: I converted a bunch of convolutional networks to jax from a lean4 base, let me know what you think: https://github.com/brettkoonce/lean4-jax/

Hi,

Some comments. I dont see the benefit of going from Lean to Jax. You cant prove semantics in Jax or are there semantic proofs on the code generation part? Furthermore when (if?) Lean Torch releases their code, then wouldnt this supercede your project (disregarding performance...)?

This just feels like switching from PyTorch API to Lean for specifying the NN, while not obtaining any additional guanrantees that Lean could power... (such as correctness of the Training Pipeline or so).
Those are valid points. I'm using more as a meta-programming tool it feels like. My lean definitions are simpler/more compact than the code used in the book.

https://github.com/ROCm/jax/issues/745 this is interesting to me. lean model definition --> jax code --> issue in the jit/rocm layer --> the formal chain exposes the error. this allows validation / consistency checking.
How did the formal chain expose the error?
lean guarantees the shapes are correct, then the jax code on top can be composed different ways --> issue is at the jit layer of how the shapes are put together

I rebuilt stuff again. Now I am going from Lean4 to MLIR and lowering to GPU via StableHLO/IREE. I am interested in particular what people think about the proof structure spelled out here: https://github.com/brettkoonce/lean4-mlir/tree/main/LeanMlir/Proofs
I rebuilt all the Proofs to use ℝ instead of Float and linked out to Mathlib proper. No more sorries!

This channel is not getting lots of attention, but at some point we will want good reasoning about fast, real-world algorithms, so I wanted to cheer you on! I think this is a promissing direction! What's your take on https://leandojo.org/torchlean.html? (As basically every mathematician that has used both, I have a soft spot for JAX, but I haven gone deeply onto the lean of any of those)

I did a talk at a conference where Anima was a headliner, definitely strong competition! My book came out and Google cancelled the S4TF library on which everything was built ~two weeks later. Despite these headwinds the theory was sound and so the book found a niche amongst researchers working in a number of different domains.

Now, I've rebuilt the primary sequence (+vit) with lean4/mlir and it's working, ~where I was at back in 2020. I'd like to push through the fiddly bits of proving the VJP structures/backprop mechanics are correct and then ship an new book.

I'm not really targeting speed/performance so much as being able to do everything in one place. With MLIR we can show literally show all the steps required to go from lean to StableHLO to IREE to the GPU. My vision is to demystify the mathematics and hopefully provide a field reference for the next generation of practitioners.
I got blueprint working, what a beautiful tool! https://brettkoonce.github.io/lean4-mlir/blueprint/
PDF: https://brettkoonce.github.io/lean4-mlir/blueprint.pdf
Brought the code/training results for the primary sequence over to blueprint + added setup instructions!

With Claude's help, ground 30 project axioms to 0 — every Jacobian now proves through Mathlib's fderiv, and the non-smooth _has_vjp shortcuts (relu_has_vjp, mlp_has_vjp, maxPool2_has_vjp3) are noncomputable defs with correct := by rfl. #print axioms vit_full_has_vjp shows only Lean core.

Worried I loosened a proof somewhere. Already passing: lake build, checkdecls, FD gradient checks, dischargeability examples. Would love a smell-check from someone who's done this before, especially on the canonical-witness pattern.
What is vjp? Canonical Witness Pattern? Something you can use to be sure that the proofs are correct is: https://github.com/leanprover/comparator/

Will give comparator a go — gotta upgrade Linux apparently. VJP: vector-Jacobian product = the backward function for a layer. Chain rule but in matrix form. Canonical witness: HasVJP f is a Lean struct of { backward, correct }. We set backward := pdiv f (which is fderiv by definition) and correct := by rfl. Works trivially. At non-smooth points fderiv returns junk-default 0 and codegen substitutes the standard subgradient/argmax — that's the only non-pure-Mathlib trust boundary.
can do a deeper pass / theorem exhaustion but the first pass with comparator didn't show anything: https://github.com/brettkoonce/lean4-mlir/tree/main/tests/comparator
Did you define this terminology yourself or is it also used in the literature? Also what is the Canonical Witness Pattern?

Furthermore if you create a Challenge.lean, maybe supplement it with more information. Why are these theorems relevant?: how do they fit in to the bigger scope (This was partially covered by the README.md), Regular Latex of the Theorem Contents. You could add these information to the docstrings of the theorems for example.

VJP is what they're called in backprop literature. Slide 21 from a talk I did shows where/how we use them: https://brettkoonce.com/presentations/introduction_to_swift_for_tensorflow_2020.pdf

structure HasVJP (f : Vec m → Vec n) where
backward : Vec m → Vec n → Vec m
correct : ∀ x dy i, backward x dy i = ∑ j, pdiv f x i j · dy j

In ML we use relu, which is defined as max(0,n). The function is continuous at 0 but its derivative isn't. For the purposes of proofs we define the gradient as 1 if n > 0 strictly, else 0. So the gradient at the kink is 0 (matches PyTorch/JAX). But then we can't easily prove correctness of this convention because at n = 0 the math has no canonical answer. So then we do this in lean:

def relu_has_vjp : HasVJP relu := {
backward := fun x dy i => ∑ j, pdiv relu x i j · dy j
correct := by rfl
}

This reduces to pdiv relu x = pdiv relu x and rfl closes it. At smooth points fderiv returns the actual derivative; at the kink it returns the junk default (0).
I explained the motivation for VJP/closed forms, O(mn) vs O(d^3): https://brettkoonce.github.io/lean4-mlir/blueprint/chap-tensor.html#a0000000013
